title: The rise and fall of teacher turnover
author: Aldeman, Chad
summary: Chad Aldeman reviews data from 21 states showing that teacher turnover spiked after the pandemic, peaked in 2022, and has since largely returned to near pre-pandemic baselines in most states. Absolute rates were never crisis-level and are comparable to other college-educated professional fields. The one persistent concern: the hardest-to-staff positions remain exactly what they were in 2019—schools serving disadvantaged students and subjects like special education, math, and science.
points: Teacher turnover followed the same broad trajectory across nearly all 21 states studied: slight decline in fall 2020, rise through reopening, peak in 2022, then gradual recovery.
Absolute turnover rates were never dramatically high—ranging from 6.2% in Pennsylvania to 15.7% in Colorado in 2025—and are comparable to other college-educated professional fields.
The pandemic-era spike tracked the broader labour market disruption rather than being an education-specific crisis, and has largely receded across most states.
Some states (Colorado, Connecticut) have fully normalised; others (Louisiana, Arkansas) show stalling recovery and merit closer attention from policymakers.
The chronic hard-to-staff gap has not closed: special education, math, and science positions, and schools serving disadvantaged students, remain as difficult to fill as before the pandemic.

But the hardest positions to staff in education are still the same ones they were in 2019: schools serving disadvantaged students and subjects like special education, math, and science.
In nearly every state for which we have data, teacher turnover declined slightly in the fall of 2020, as many public schools remained remote and the broader economy was frozen.
Policymakers in the latter group of states should be more worried, especially if teacher turnover rates continue to stall at a permanently higher plateau.
Colorado and Connecticut are fully back to normal, while Louisiana’s chart is bouncing around and Arkansas’ rate of improvement has slowed considerably.
Teacher turnover did spike after the pandemic, but the latest data suggest that spike was fairly consistent across states, and it has largely receded.
Every state has seen turnover fall from its pandemic-era peak, although the trends look different depending on where you live.
